newsitem.title: UK: UK supermarkets want gene-bean issue clarified.
newsitem.headline: UK supermarkets want gene-bean issue clarified.

text.p: Major British supermarkets called on Monday for more information and greater choice over using genetically-modified soybeans but said they consider the products safe.
A spokesman for supermarket chain J.Sainsbury Plc said the British retail community was "disappointed" that modified soya would come to Britain in 1997 and had lobbied against it.
"But it's been okayed by the Department of the Environment and it's coming over. Our hands are tied," he said.

Monsanto Co of the United States has developed the modified bean to resist the herbicide Roundup which it also produces. The Greenpeace environmentalist group has led a protest against exports of the beans, now starting, to Europe.
The supermarkets' chief objection is that difficulties in distinguishing between modified beans and maincrop product restricts consumer choice and causes labelling problems.
Iceland Plc, a freezer-fare retailer, cited consumer "mistrust" over what it called unnatural processes in a letter to Greenpeace this week.
The top five UK supermarkets said they had only received a limited number of queries from customers over the issue.
Sainsbury's and Asda said they were actively working with suppliers to source soybeans, distinguish between the types and provide full information to customers.
Iceland's letter to Greenpeace said it felt Monsanto had acted irresponsibly in letting the beans into the marketplace.

"Iceland and its suppliers have some choice in the market-place but as Monsanto are by far the largest and most competitive supplier of the soybeans in the world market it makes the position very difficult," it said.
Iceland said that it was highly unlikely that the company would be selling genetically-modified soy products next year.
But other stores said they had checked with suppliers and none could guarantee to supply unmodified soyproducts because the beans were mixed with the maincrop at the point of origin.
One supermarket said it was actively seeking access to technology that would be able to distinguish between the beans in finished products.
Another said it had enough stocks of non-modified product to last well into 1997 and hoped that the issue would be resolved by the time it ran out.
Sainsbury's said its stores had been targeted by environmental protestors over the weekend.
"We thought it was a bit unfair because we're in the same boat as them, we want to be able to label the products," a spokesman said. "This is a global problem."
In a related development, some British scientists expressed concern over a new form of genetically-modified corn (maize) produced by Ciba-Geigy for use in cattle feed.
Government biotechnology adviser Professor Derek Burke told BBC television on Sunday that the feed could lead to increased resistance to antibiotics in humans.
